results.title: Benjamini-Hochberg Correction - MetricGate Calculator
results.content: Try our Benjamini-Hochberg Calculator to control the false discovery rate in your multiple hypothesis tests. # Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure (False Discovery Rate Control) ## Overview The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is a powerful method for controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR) in multiple hypothesis testing. Unlike the Bonferroni or Holm corrections, which control the probability of any false positives (family-wise error rate), the BH procedure focuses on controlling the expected proportion of false positives among all rejected hypotheses. ## How It Works Suppose you run *m* hypothesis tests and obtain p-values *p(1), ..., p(m)* sorted in ascending order. 2. For each p-value *p(i)*, calculate the threshold: mi​⋅α. The BH procedure is especially suited to exploratory research and large-scale testing scenarios where FDR control is more appropriate than family-wise error rate control. ## R Code Example Suppose you have six p-values: p=[0.005,0.01,0.04,0.08,0.12,0.20] With α=0.05 and *m = 6* tests, the BH threshold for each rank *i* is 6i​⋅0.05. Run this code in the MetricGate R Workspace to see how the BH correction works: # Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction Example in R # Simulated p-values from 6 hypothesis tests raw_pvalues <- c(0.005, 0.01, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.20) # Apply BH correction bh_adjusted <- p.adjust(raw_pvalues, method = "BH") # Compile results Test = paste0("H", 1:6), # Print results # Optional visualization col = ifelse(results$Significant, "red", "gray"), main = "Benjamini-Hochberg Adjusted P-values" abline(h = 0.05, col = "blue", lty = 2) legend("topright", legend = c("Significant", "Not Significant"), fill = c("red", "gray")) ## Interpreting Results After applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, two hypotheses (H1 and H2) are flagged as statistically significant at the 5% FDR threshold. * **Significant:** H1 and H2 have BH-adjusted p-values of 0.03 → we reject the null hypothesis for these comparisons, controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries. * **Not Significant:** H3 to H6 have adjusted p-values between 0.08 and 0.20 → we do not reject their null hypotheses. This demonstrates the strength of BH correction: it allows more discoveries (H1 and H2) than stricter methods like Bonferroni, while still controlling the false discovery rate across all comparisons. ## Limitations * **Does not guarantee zero false positives:** It controls the proportion, not the presence, of false discoveries.

results.title: Familywise Error Rate (Alpha Inflation): Definition - Statistics How To
results.content: # Familywise Error Rate (Alpha Inflation): Definition. Post Hoc tests > Familywise Error Rate. ## What is the Familywise Error Rate? The **familywise error rate** (FWE or FWER) is the probability of a coming to at least one false conclusion in a series of hypothesis tests . The term “familywise” error rate comes from *family of tests*, which is the technical definition for a series of tests on data. The FWER is also called *alpha inflation* or *cumulative Type I error*. The formula to estimate the familywise error rate is:. * αIT = alpha level for an individual test (e.g. For example, with an alpha level of 5% and a series of ten tests, the FWER is:. This means that the probability of a type I error is just over 40%, which is very high considering only ten tests were performed. You need to control the FWER for one main reason: If you run enough hypothesis tests (dozens, hundreds, or sometimes tens of thousands) you’re *highly likely* to get at least one significant result—a “false alarm” where you incorrectly reject the null hypothesis. Two main procedures are used to control the FWER: single step and sequential. The single step procedure makes equal adjustments to each p-value. 1. Divide the alpha level by the number of tests you’re running and apply that alpha level to each individual test. For example, if your overall alpha level is .05 and you are running 5 tests, then each test will have an alpha level of .05/5 = .01. 2. Apply the new alpha level to each test for finding p-values. The Bonferroni correction has been criticized for (among other things) loss of power and a high probability of Type II errors. Similar to Bonferroni, but makes adaptive adjustments to each p-value. 1. **Holm-Bonferroni**: tests are run and then ordered from lowest to highest p-values. The individual tests are then tested (starting with the one with the lowest p-value) with an overall Bonferroni correction for all tests. See: *Holm-Bonferroni Method* for a step-by-step example. results.title: Unplanned Comparisons | Real Statistics Using Excel
results.content: We will review the most useful tests here. Although many tests are available, it is important to avoid the temptation to perform multiple tests and select the results that are most favorable to whatever you are trying to prove. You should select one of these tests, and stick with it, possibly using another test to gain some further insight. Fortunately, there are criteria to follow that make one test more appropriate than another. Since multiple (usually pairwise) comparisons are performed, a key objective of all these tests is to control familywise error. Although the Bonferroni and Dunn/Sidák correction factors can be used, since we are considering unplanned tests, we must assume that all pairwise tests will be made (or at least taken into account). For *k* groups, this results in *m* = *C*(*k*, 2) = *k*(*k*–1)/2 tests. For an experiment-wise error of α we need to use *α*/*m* as the alpha for each test (Bonferroni) or 1 – (1 – *α*)1/*m* (Dunn/ Sidák). This makes these tests too conservative. More useful tests are Tukey’s HSD and REGWQ. These tests are designed only for pairwise comparisons (i.e. no complex contrasts). We also describe extensions to Tukey’s HSD test (Tukey-Kramer and Games and Howell) where the sample sizes or variances are unequal. We also describe the Scheffé test, which can be used for non-pairwise comparisons. * Tukey’s HSD test is usually the safe choice. * REGWQ test is even better (i.e. has more power) for comparing all pairs of means, but should not be used when group sizes are different. * Benjamini-Hochberg is best when sample sizes are very different or where there are a very large number of tests. * Dunnett’s test is useful when you only want to make comparisons with a single control group. * Hsu’s MCB test is useful when you only want to make comparisons with the group with either the highest or lowest mean. * Tukey’s LSD test has high power but at the cost of not protecting against familywise test error. Click on any of the following post-hoc tests for further information:. * General pairwise tests (Bonferroni, Dunn-Sidàk, Holm, Hochberg, Benjamini-Hochberg, Benjamini-Yekutieli).
